1:1.headline: Petuel: the Rabbis read it as Samuel, who won God over
1:1.body: Rashi says Petuel is Samuel the prophet, named for how he persuaded God (פיתה לאל) with his prayer. Ibn Ezra says that by the plain meaning Joel is not Samuel's son.

sources.quote: בֶּן שְׁמוּאֵל הַנָּבִיא, שֶׁפִּתָּה לָאֵל בִּתְפִלָּתוֹ
sources.says: Rashi says he is the son of Samuel the prophet, who persuaded God with his prayer.

sources.quote: ארז״ל זה שמואל הנביא שפיתה לאל בתפילתו
sources.says: Metzudat David says the Rabbis identify him as Samuel, who persuaded God with his prayer.

sources.quote: ולפי הפשט איננו בן שמואל
sources.says: Ibn Ezra says that by the plain meaning he is not Samuel's son.

1:4.headline: ילק: the locust that licks the grass bare
1:4.body: Radak and Ibn Ezra explain the name ילק from לקק, "to lick": it licks up the grass with its tongue.

sources.quote: וילק לפי שהוא לוקק ולוחך את העשב
sources.says: Radak says ילק is so called because it licks and laps up the grass.

sources.quote: וילק שילוק בלשונו
sources.says: Ibn Ezra says ילק is named for licking with its tongue.

1:4.headline: חסיל: the locust that finishes off what is left
1:4.body: Radak and Malbim tie the name חסיל to Deuteronomy 28:38, "the locust shall consume it" (יחסלנו). It is the last swarm, and it eats everything.

sources.quote: וחסיל לפי שהוא כורת את הכל מן יחסלנו הארבה
sources.says: Radak says חסיל is so called because it cuts down everything, from "the locust shall consume it".

sources.quote: והחסיל אוכל את הכל, כמו כי יחסלנו הארבה
sources.says: Malbim says the חסיל eats everything, as in "the locust shall consume it".

1:6.headline: A "nation" of locusts
1:6.body: גוי usually means a nation of people. Rashi says the prophet calls the locust swarm a nation, like an army. Radak says any gathering of living things can be called this, as Proverbs calls ants a "people".

sources.quote: הַגּוֹבַאי הַזֶּה כִּנָּהוּ כְּצָבָא גּוֹי
sources.says: Rashi says the prophet calls this locust a nation, like an army.

sources.quote: כל קבוץ מן החי יקרא גוי לפיכך אמר על הארבה גוי, וכן אמר על הנמלים עם לא עז
sources.says: Radak says any group of living things is called גוי, so the locust is called one, as ants are called "a people not strong".

1:7.headline: לקצפה: the fig tree turned to grief, to a curse, or to bark
1:7.body: קצף usually means anger. Metzudat Zion reads the fig tree as cursed and Rashi as a cause of grief. Radak cites others who read peeled bark, and Malbim says a peeled fig tree oozes foam.

sources.quote: לִקְצָפָה. לְמַפַּח נֶפֶשׁ
sources.says: Rashi says it means to grief and despair.

sources.quote: לקצפה. מל׳ קצף ור״ל למארה
sources.says: Metzudat Zion says it is from the word for anger, meaning a curse.

sources.quote: וי"מ לקצפה לקליפה וכן מפרשים כקצף על פני המים
sources.says: Radak says some explain it as peeling, and read "like קצף on the water" (Hosea 10:7) the same way.

sources.quote: לקצפה - כמו קצף על פני מים שאין בו ממש
sources.says: Ibn Ezra says it is like foam on water, with nothing solid in it.

sources.quote: התאנה הנקלפה תעלה קצף ואבעבועות
sources.says: Malbim says a peeled fig tree gives off foam and bubbles.

1:8.headline: The young widow is also a vine that was never pruned
1:8.body: Radak reads a young bride mourning the husband she married in her youth. Malbim adds that the Rabbis call a tree never cut a "virgin": the stripped vine, wrapped in sacking, mourns its lost branches like a husband.

sources.quote: כמו הבתולה שנשאת לבחור ומת בעודה נערה
sources.says: Radak says she is like a young woman who married a young man and he died while she was still a girl.

sources.quote: ובפי החכמים יקרא האילן שלא נקצץ מימיו בשם בתולה
sources.says: Malbim says the Rabbis call a tree that was never cut a virgin.

sources.quote: ויקרא הענפים שקצצו ממנה בשם בעל, כי הם למעלה ממנה
sources.says: Malbim says the branches cut from the vine are called its husband, because they are above it.

sources.quote: והמנהג לחבוש שק על הגזע שהוסר הקליפה ממנו
sources.says: Malbim says the custom was to wrap sacking around a trunk whose bark was stripped.

1:10.headline: Does the ground mourn, or wither?
1:10.body: אבל usually means mourning. Metzudat Zion and Radak read the ground as ruined, with no fruit, and the Targum says "the land is laid waste". Ibn Ezra reads it as the people living on the ground mourning.

sources.quote: אבלה. ענין השחתה כמו אבל תירוש
sources.says: Metzudat Zion says אבלה means ruin, as in "the new wine withers" (Isaiah 24).

sources.quote: נשחתה ושממה. כי אין בה פירות
sources.says: Radak says the ground is ruined and desolate, with no fruit.

sources.quote: חֲרוּבַת אַרְעָא
sources.says: The Targum renders it "the land is laid waste".

sources.quote: אבלה אדמה - הטעם אבלו יושביה
sources.says: Ibn Ezra says it means the people living on it mourned.

1:12.headline: Why the vine "dries" but the fig is "cut off"
1:12.body: Metzudat Zion and Rashi say אמללה means cut off. Malbim explains the change of word: a cut vine grows back from its root, but a fig tree does not, so the fig is lost for good.

sources.quote: אמללה. נכרתה
sources.says: Metzudat Zion says אמללה means cut off.

sources.quote: נִכְרְתָה פָּסַק פִּרְיָהּ
sources.says: Rashi says it was cut off and its fruit stopped.

sources.quote: הגפן הנקצץ יצמח שנית משרשו, לא כן התאנה כנודע, לכן אמר שהתאנה אומללה לגמרי
sources.says: Malbim says a cut vine grows again from its root but a fig does not, so the verse says the fig is wholly cut off.

1:17.headline: עבשו: a word found only here, for going moldy
1:17.body: Ibn Ezra says the word appears nowhere else. Radak and Metzudat Zion read it as עפשו, "moldy", since ב and פ are said with the lips alike. Malbim also suggests באשו, "stank", with the letters moved around.

sources.quote: עבשו - אין לו חבר
sources.says: Ibn Ezra says עבשו has no other example.

sources.quote: כמו עפשו ענין עפוש כי הבי"ת והפ"א ממוצא אחד
sources.says: Radak says it is like עפשו, mold, because bet and peh are made in the same place in the mouth.

sources.quote: כמו עפשו בפ״א ולשון עפוש ידוע בדרז״ל
sources.says: Metzudat Zion says it is like עפשו with a peh, a word for mold known from the Rabbis.

sources.quote: ועבשו כמו באשו בחילוף התיבות
sources.says: Malbim suggests עבשו may be באשו, "stank", with the letters swapped.

1:17.headline: פרדות: wine jars under their lids, or seeds under the clods
1:17.body: The Targum and Rashi read wine jars gone moldy under their stoppers. Radak and Ibn Ezra read seeds rotting in the ground under clods of earth.

sources.quote: פְּרֻדּוֹת. תִּרְגֵּם יוֹנָתָן ״גַּרְבֵּי חַמְרָא״
sources.says: Rashi says the Targum renders פרדות as "jars of wine".

sources.quote: מְגוּפַת כִּסּוּי הֶחָבִיּוֹת
sources.says: Rashi says the מגרפות are the stoppers that cover the jars.

sources.quote: פרדות. הם גרגרי הזרע שהם תחת הארץ
sources.says: Radak says פרדות are the seed grains under the ground.

sources.quote: והם חתיכות העפר
sources.says: Radak says the מגרפות are clods of earth.

sources.quote: פרודות הם גרגרי החטה והשעורה הזרועים
sources.says: Ibn Ezra cites Rabbi Marinus: פרודות are the sown grains of wheat and barley.

1:18.headline: Did the sheep sin? נאשמו as "made desolate" or "held guilty"
1:18.body: Radak and Metzudat David read it as desolate, as in Hosea. Malbim reads it as guilt, and hears a protest: why are the flocks punished when people sinned?

sources.quote: וענינו ענין שממה וכן תאשם שומרון
sources.says: Radak says it means desolation, as in "Samaria shall be desolate".

sources.quote: נאשמו. נעשו שממה וחורבן
sources.says: Metzudat David says they became desolate and ruined.

sources.quote: נאשמו. מענין חטא ואשמה
sources.says: Malbim says נאשמו is from sin and guilt.

sources.quote: הכי חטאו גם המה ויאשמו אשום? ולמה ענש ה' את הבהמה
sources.says: Malbim says the prophet asks whether the flocks also sinned, and why God punished the animals.

2:8.headline: Falling on the sword, or falling on God's errand
2:8.body: Radak reads השלח as a sword: the locusts land on blades and are not hurt. The Targum reads it from שליחות, a mission: they throw themselves wherever God sends them.

sources.quote: השלח הוא הסייף
sources.says: Radak says השלח is the sword.

sources.quote: וְיוֹנָתָן פָּתַר בּוֹ לְשׁוֹן ׳שְׁלִיחוּת׳ בִּשְׁבִיל שְׁלִיחוּת שֶׁל הַקָּדוֹשׁ בָּרוּךְ הוּא מַפִּילִין עַצְמָן
sources.says: Rashi says the Targum reads it as a mission: they throw themselves down for God's errand.

2:8.headline: They are not wounded, or they take no bribe
2:8.body: Radak reads יבצעו like יפצעו, they are not cut. Rashi and the Targum hear בצע, money: unlike human armies, these cannot be paid off.

sources.quote: לא יבצעו. כמו לא יפצעו
sources.says: Radak says it means they are not wounded, and notes the Targum reads it as hating gain.

sources.quote: וְלֹא יְקַבְּלוּן מָמוֹן
sources.says: Rashi says it means they will not accept money.

2:13.headline: Tear your hearts, not your clothes
2:13.body: Tearing clothes was the usual sign of grief. Ibn Ezra says tearing the heart means removing its covering so it can understand, like 'circumcise your heart'.

sources.quote: והנה הטעם להסיר מכסה לב לקורעו, כי הוא ימנע שלא יבין הלב
sources.says: Ibn Ezra says tearing the heart means removing its covering, which stops the heart from understanding.

sources.quote: פתחו והסירו ערלת לבבכם להראות הכנעה
sources.says: Metzudat Zion says it means open and remove the covering of your heart, to show humility.

2:18.headline: God becomes zealous for His land, or issues a warning
2:18.body: Rashi first reads ויקנא as zeal: the land's pain entered God's heart and He fought for it. He then brings the sages' reading of the word as a warning.

sources.quote: נִכְנְסָה בְּלִבּוֹ צָרָתָהּ וְנִלְחַם בְּמִלְחַמְתָּהּ
sources.says: Rashi says the land's trouble entered God's heart and He fought its battle.

sources.quote: וְרַבּוֹתֵינוּ פֵּרְשׁוּ לְשׁוֹן ׳הַתְרָאָה׳
sources.says: Rashi adds that the sages explain the word as a warning.

2:20.headline: The northerner, or the one hidden in the heart
2:20.body: Plainly הצפוני is the locust army that came from the north. The sages hear צפון, hidden: the evil urge hidden in a person's heart, which God will drive away.

sources.quote: הארבה קרא צפוני שבא להם מפאת צפון
sources.says: Radak says the locust is called the northerner because it came from the north.

sources.quote: וְרַבּוֹתֵינוּ אוֹמְרִים זֶה יֵצֶר הָרָע שֶׁצָּפוּן בִּלְבָבוֹ שֶׁל אָדָם
sources.says: Rashi brings the plain reading, a reading about Assyria, and the sages' reading that it is the evil urge hidden in the heart.

2:26.headline: The shame of chapter one is reversed
2:26.body: God promises that His people will never יבשו, be ashamed. Ibn Ezra hears it as the reverse of 1:11, where the farmers הובישו. He notes the two words come from different roots but mean the same.

sources.quote: הפך הובישו אכרים והם שנים שרשים והטעם אחד
sources.says: Ibn Ezra says this is the opposite of 'the farmers were shamed', from two roots with one meaning.

4:2.headline: The Valley of Jehoshaphat: named for a king, or for "God judges"
4:2.body: Rashi reads the name as "God's judgment", since God judges the nations there. Radak says it may be named after King Jehoshaphat or after the judging; Ibn Ezra calls the "God judges" reading a sermon, not the plain sense.

sources.quote: ארד עמם בעמק הדין, יהושפט משפטי יה
sources.says: Rashi says God will go down with them into the valley of judgment, since Yehoshafat means "the judgment of God".

sources.quote: וזה העמק היה למלך יהושפט אולי בנה שם או עשה שם מעשה ונקרא על שמו
sources.says: Radak says this valley belonged to King Jehoshaphat, perhaps because he built or did something there, and it was named after him.

sources.quote: או נקרא עמק יהושפט על שם המשפט. כמו שאמר ונשפטתי עמם שם
sources.says: Radak says it may be called the Valley of Jehoshaphat after the judgment, as the verse says "I will judge them there".

sources.quote: והמפרש יהושפט כי השם ישפטם, זה דרך דרש הוא
sources.says: Ibn Ezra says that explaining Jehoshaphat as "God will judge them" is a sermon reading.

4:4.headline: Gemul: paying someone back, or starting the harm
4:4.body: Radak and Metzudat Zion say גמול can mean the first act of good or harm, or paying it back. God asks Tyre and Sidon: are you repaying Me for something, or starting a fight with Me?

sources.quote: וגמול הוא תחלת הטובה שמטיב אדם לחבירו או תחלת הרעה
sources.says: Radak says gemul is the first good a person does to another, or the first harm.

sources.quote: וכשנקשר הענין בלשון שלום הוא להשבת גמול
sources.says: Radak says that when the word is joined to "paying", it means paying back.

sources.quote: גם תחילת המעשה יקרא בלשון גמול
sources.says: Metzudat Zion says the beginning of an act is also called gemul.

sources.quote: זהו הגמול שנתן שלמה לחירם מלך צור עשרים עיר
sources.says: Rashi says God asks if this is their thanks for the twenty cities Solomon gave Hiram, king of Tyre.

4:11.headline: Ushu: a word found only here, read four ways
4:11.body: Rashi cites Menachem, "hurry", and the Aramaic, "gather"; he himself links it to a mass of iron. Radak and Ibn Ezra take it from עש, a cluster of stars, and Malbim from moths, weak things gathered together.

sources.quote: עושו. כמו ׳חושו׳ כך חברו מנחם. ויונתן תרגם ״יתכנשון״, ואומר אני שהוא לשון ׳עשת ברזל׳ המכנס יחד
sources.says: Rashi says Menachem grouped it with "chushu", hurry, Targum Jonathan translates "gather", and Rashi links it to "eshet barzel", a mass of iron pressed together.

sources.quote: הקבצו מן עש כסיל וכימה שהוא חבור כוכבים
sources.says: Radak says it means "gather", from "ash", a cluster of stars, like Orion and the Pleiades.

sources.quote: התקבצו ומגזרת עיש שהם ז' כוכבים, לעולם לא יתפרדו
sources.says: Ibn Ezra says it means gather, from "ayish", seven stars that never separate.

sources.quote: מענין אסיפה ואין לו ריע, וענינו אסיפת דברים חלשים כעש ונמלים
sources.says: Malbim says it means gathering and has no parallel, and it is the gathering of weak things like moths and ants.

4:11.headline: "Bring down Your mighty ones": God's angels, or the enemy's heroes
4:11.body: Ibn Ezra and Radak say the prophet asks God to bring down His mighty ones, the angels. Rashi follows the Aramaic: there God will break the nations' might.

sources.quote: גבוריך - שם, והם המלאכים
sources.says: Ibn Ezra says "your mighty ones" are the angels.

sources.quote: גבוריך. הם המלאכים
sources.says: Radak says "your mighty ones" are the angels.

sources.quote: שם בקבוצת עמק יהושפט ישבור גבורתכם כן תרגם יונתן
sources.says: Rashi says that there, at the gathering in the Valley of Jehoshaphat, God will break your might, as Targum Jonathan translates.

4:13.headline: "Come, go down": or come and tread the grapes
4:13.body: Radak reads רדו as going down into the valley, which is like a full winepress. Rashi reads it as treading and pressing, as in "rule over the fish of the sea" (Genesis 1:28).

sources.quote: רדו בעמק הזה כי הוא כמו הגת שמלאה ענבים
sources.says: Radak says it means go down into this valley, for it is like a winepress full of grapes.

sources.quote: רדו לשון כבישה ורדוי כמו ״ורדו בדגת הים״
sources.says: Rashi says "redu" means pressing down and ruling, as in "rule over the fish of the sea".

4:14.headline: The Valley of Decision: where the nations are cut down, or judged
4:14.body: Radak says it is called "cut" because the nations are cut down there, or because their sentence is cut and decided. Malbim says the same valley is called Jehoshaphat while the trial runs and Charutz once the verdict is final.

sources.quote: קורא אותו חרוץ כי שם יהיו הגוים חרוצים וחתוכים, או כי שם יחרוץ ויחתוך משפטם
sources.says: Radak says it is called charutz because there the nations will be cut and chopped, or because there their sentence will be decided.

sources.quote: כי עמק יהושפט נקרא בעת המשפט, שאז חוקר על דינם
sources.says: Malbim says it is called the Valley of Jehoshaphat while the judgment is under way and their case is examined.

sources.quote: אבל אז יקרא בשם עמק החרוץ, שכבר נחרץ ונגמר הדין שהם חייבים כליה
sources.says: Malbim says then it is called the Valley of Decision, because the verdict is already decided that they deserve destruction.

4:16.headline: God roars from Zion, but only "gives voice" from Jerusalem
4:16.body: Malbim says roaring is much louder than giving voice. Zion, the holier place, gets the roar, and the rest of Jerusalem gets the quieter voice.

sources.quote: שאגה גדולה מנתינת קול
sources.says: Malbim says roaring is greater than giving voice.

sources.quote: ובירושלים שאינה קדושה כציון הגם שלא ישאג בקול גדול בכ"ז לא ידום רק יתן קולו
sources.says: Malbim says that in Jerusalem, which is not as holy as Zion, God will not roar loudly, but He will not be silent either: He will give voice.

4:16.headline: "From Zion he roars": from His home, or because of Zion
4:16.body: Radak says God's presence is in Jerusalem, so it is as if He roars from there. Rashi reads "from Zion" as "because of": He roars over what the nations did to Zion.

sources.quote: כי שם שכינתו בירושלם וכאלו משם ישאג ויתן קולו עליהם
sources.says: Radak says God's presence is there in Jerusalem, so it is as if He roars and gives voice against them from there.

sources.quote: מציון ישאג. ממה שעשו לציון
sources.says: Rashi says "from Zion He roars" means because of what they did to Zion.

4:21.headline: "I will clear them, but their blood I will not clear"
4:21.body: Rashi and Radak say God may forgive the nations other wrongs, like stolen silver and gold, but not the blood of Judah they shed. Malbim reads it the other way: God will now also avenge the blood He had not yet avenged.

sources.quote: ואף אם אנקה אותם משאר עבירות שבידם ומרעות שעשו לי, דמם של בני יהודה לא אנקה מהם
sources.says: Rashi says that even if God clears them of their other sins and the wrongs they did Him, He will not clear them of the blood of Judah.

sources.quote: מכספם וזהבם שלקחו אנקה האומות
sources.says: Radak says God will clear the nations of the silver and gold they took.

sources.quote: אבל דמם ששפכו לא אנקה אותם
sources.says: Radak says that for the blood they shed He will not clear them.

sources.quote: אומר שאח"כ אנקה גם את דמם אשר לא נקיתי עדיין במפלת גוג
sources.says: Malbim says that afterward God will also avenge their blood which He had not yet avenged in the fall of Gog.
